115485.etyen:
From graut (“porridge; thick, soft mass”) + -e (“verb-forming suffix”). The base noun graut continues Old Norse grautr (“porridge”) and is related to gryte (“pot, cooking pot”).
In the historical Telemark sense, the verb referred to visiting a woman after childbirth while bringing her porridge. The custom and visit itself were called grauting (“traditional postpartum porridge visit”), while the visiting women were known as grautkjerringer (“porridge women”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk graute (“to cook porridge; knead or stir together”).

en.g: a constituent country of the United Kingdom

1001501.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Skotland, from Skota (“of the Scots”), the genitive plural of skotr (“Scot”), and land (“land, country”); literally “land of the Scots”. The ethnonym skotr has been compared with Old or Middle Irish scott (“Irishman”) and may be an early borrowing from it, though the connection is uncertain. The wider ethnonym is also represented by Late Latin Scotus (“Irishman, Gael”); its ultimate origin is unknown.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Skottland, Swedish Skottland, Danish Skotland, Icelandic Skotland and Faroese Skotland (“Scotland”).

en.g: a lake in Oppdal, Trøndelag, Norway, forming the source of the river Orkla

1004573.etyen:
Continues an older lake name reconstructed as Old Norse *Orkill or *Orkull, formed from the river name *Ork with the archaic lake-name suffix -ill or -ull. The present form includes sjøen (“the lake”) as an explanatory addition. Ultimately unknown.
The underlying river name has traditionally been connected with orka (“to work, labour”), perhaps referring to a strong current, while an Old European origin has also been proposed; both interpretations are uncertain.
Compare Sperillen, from Old Norse Sperðill, another old Norwegian lake name containing the suffix -ill.
